title: In 1494, two countries split the world in half
sources: Treaty of Tordesillas signed 7 June 1494 by Spain (Ferdinand II and Isabella I) and Portugal (John II); line moved to 370 leagues west of Cape Verde, about 46°30′W; the 1493 papal line (Pope Alexander VI) ran 100 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands; Brazil juts across the line; local populations were not considered at all: World History Encyclopedia, 'Treaty of Tordesillas' (https://worldhistory.org/Treaty_of_Tordesillas)
Cabral's fleet of thirteen ships reached Brazil on 22 April 1500, near today's Porto Seguro, and claimed it for Portugal: History Today, 'Cabral Discovers Brazil'
Brazil 213.4 million people (IBGE estimate, July 2025); Portugal about 10.7 million: 213.4 / 10.7 ≈ 20
Most of South America speaks Spanish; Guyana (English), Suriname (Dutch) and French Guiana (French) are the other exceptions, so the script says 'most'
The 1493 line is drawn at about 38°W, as on common reconstructions; its exact position is debated, so the video doesn't state it

script.say: In 1494, two countries split the whole world in half.
script.speak: In fourteen ninety-four, two countries split the whole world in half.
script.speakNatural: In fourteen ninety-four, two countries split the whole world in half.

script.say: Spain and Portugal were racing to claim new lands across the ocean.
So the Pope drew a line down the Atlantic. West of it, Spain. East of it, Portugal.
Portugal pushed back. And in 1494, at a town called Tordesillas, they moved the line further west.
script.speak: Portugal pushed back. And in fourteen ninety-four, at a town called Tordesillas, they moved the line further west.
script.speakNatural: Portugal pushed back. And in fourteen ninety-four, at a town called Tor-de-see-yas, they moved the line further west.

script.say: Nobody in Europe knew it yet, but that new line cut through a land they had never seen.
Six years later, a Portuguese fleet landed right there.
That's why Brazil speaks Portuguese, while most of South America speaks Spanish.
Brazil later grew far beyond the line.
And the people already living there? Nobody asked them.
Today, Brazil has over two hundred million people. Twenty times the population of Portugal.
